title: How To Rid Your Classroom Of Excitability
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that classroom excitability—fidgeting, distraction, and inability to focus—is caused not by students but by the teacher's own energy, which students absorb and mirror. He explains that students respect and settle around a genuinely calm, unhurried presence, while a harried or nervous teacher's energy 'rubs off' and amplifies restlessness regardless of the intended message. He acknowledges that nervousness before the school day is normal, but insists it must be released the moment the morning bell rings, treating classroom composure as a performance a teacher steps into. The piece closes by framing calm presence as the gateway to freely expressing a teacher's authentic personality and influence.
points: Classroom excitability is attributed primarily to the teacher's own temperament rather than something students inherently bring with them.
Students take on and mirror the emotional energy—calm or anxious—of their teacher, even when the teacher believes it isn't showing.
A consistently calm teacher earns a form of respect students rarely encounter from other adults, which itself reduces misbehavior.
Pre-class nervousness is normal, but it must be consciously released the moment the school day begins.
Calm presence is framed as the precondition for a teacher's authentic personality and influence to come through fully.
quotes: Spend a day visiting classrooms at your neighborhood school and you’ll find many buzzing with tension.
A consistently tense and excitable classroom is caused not by students, but by their teacher.
A consistently calm personality shows a leadership quality lacking in most adults students come in contact with, and they immediately respect it.
Students tend to take on the personality of their teacher. Outsiders can see this just by spending a few minutes in their company—even out of your presence.
For anxiety and stress have no place in a well-run classroom. They are saboteurs of the highest order, spawning excitability, misbehavior, unhappiness, and a teacher wound too tight to be effective.
